introduction: These hundred readings are about one country. Bahá’u’lláh and above all ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, writing and speaking in the years of the Constitutional Revolution and the First World War, recall Iran's ancient greatness, grieve over its ruin, say that counsel was given and not heard, blame faction and ignorant leadership, and promise that the land where the new light first rose will one day be the envy of the world. The passages beside them include Persia as other scriptures saw it, from Cyrus the Lord's anointed to the wise men from the east; Persian poets known everywhere, Sa‘di, Rumi and Khayyam; and prophets and poets of other nations on ruin, awakening and restoration: Isaiah, Jeremiah and Nehemiah, Tagore, Yeats, Lincoln, Burke. A few ask what national memory is for, what a country should take from the West, and on what hope rests.
questions: The readings remind Iranians of an ancient greatness. What is the use, and what is the danger, of a nation remembering its past glories?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that counsel was given to the country's statesmen and not heard. Why is advice from one's own so often refused?
The readings blame parties and faction for the country's ruin; Washington grants that parties have their uses within limits. What have you seen faction do to a community?
One reading rejects mere imitation of the West, and Gandhi distrusts Western civilization altogether. What should any country borrow, and what should it grow from its own roots?
Wordsworth and Dickens remember the hope and the terror of a revolution. What changes a country more deeply than a change of government?
The readings are sure that Iran's winter will end. What grounds for hope about your own country would you offer to someone who doubts?

outside.why: Isaiah speaks of a Persian king as the Lord's anointed: thus saith the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden.
The Book of Ezra preserves the decree of Cyrus king of Persia, who sent the exiles home to rebuild their temple.
Jesus told his followers: ye are the light of the world; a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Isaiah calls to a people: arise, shine, for thy light is come.
The Qur’an teaches its Prophet to pray: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.
Tennyson, in the first age of railways, cried: forward, forward let us range; let the great world spin for ever down the ringing grooves of change.
Thoreau, watching a railway being built, called such inventions improved means to an unimproved end. What must accompany railways and commerce for a country to be truly advanced?
Proverbs says that righteousness exalteth a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.
Jesus said that unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
Jesus said that no prophet is accepted in his own country. Why should the land where a light first rose be slower than others to benefit from it?
The exiled psalmist says: if I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
Omar Khayyam wrote: they say the lion and the lizard keep the courts where Jamshyd gloried and drank deep.
Shelley's traveller found in the desert the wreck of a statue of a king of kings. What is the use of a nation remembering a greatness that is gone?
Daniel read the writing on the wall to the king of Babylon: thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.
In the Persian court of the Book of Esther, Mordecai asks the queen who knows whether she is come to the kingdom for such a time as this.
Lamentations begins: how doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people; she that was great among the nations.
Matthew Arnold described himself as wandering between two worlds, one dead, the other powerless to be born. How does a people live between a remembered past and a future not yet arrived?
Sa‘di of Shiraz wrote that kings exist for protecting subjects: the sheep is not for the shepherd, but the shepherd for the service of it.
The Preacher says: one generation passeth away, and another generation cometh, but the earth abideth for ever.
The psalm asks that what the fathers have told be shown to the generation to come.
Matthew's Gospel tells of wise men from the east who came to Jerusalem following a star.
Through Isaiah God says: for a small moment have I forsaken thee, but with great mercies will I gather thee.
Isaiah says that the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
Haggai promises that the glory of the latter house shall be greater than of the former.
Isaiah says: they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations.
Sa‘di wrote the lines for which Persian letters are best known abroad: the sons of Adam are limbs of each other, having been created of one essence.
Rumi begins his great poem with a reed-flute lamenting its banishment from its home.
Paul tells those newly grafted into an old tree: boast not against the branches. How should a people speak of a distinction it has received and others have shared?
Isaiah says to his own nation: your country is desolate; your land, strangers devour it in your presence.
Nehemiah, cupbearer to a Persian king, showed his people their ruined city, and they said: let us rise up and build.
Emerson wrote that imitation is suicide, and that a man must take himself for better, for worse, as his portion.
Gandhi wrote of the civilization of the modern West that one has only to be patient and it will be self-destroyed. What should a country take from the West, and what should it decline?
Mary Wollstonecraft wrote: strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.
Jesus said that the harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few.
Tagore prayed for his own country: where the mind is without fear and the head is held high, into that heaven of freedom let my country awake.
FitzGerald's Omar Khayyam opens with the word Wake, as the sun strikes the Sultan's turret with a shaft of light.
Paul says: now it is high time to awake out of sleep; the night is far spent, the day is at hand.
Montesquieu's Persian visitor to Paris marvelled that the French run and fly, unlike the measured step of his own country. Is the wakefulness of the West the kind of awakening the readings hope for?
The Letter to the Ephesians quotes: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead.
Proverbs asks: how long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? When wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?
Jesus wept over Jerusalem, saying: if thou hadst known, in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace.
Jesus lamented: how often would I have gathered thy children together, and ye would not.
Jeremiah speaks for his people: the harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.
Proverbs says that where no counsel is, the people fall, but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Ezekiel was told to speak whether they would hear or whether they would forbear.
Socrates told Athens that he was a gadfly given to the state by God, always arousing, persuading and reproaching.
Isaiah was sent to a people who hear indeed, but understand not.
Jeremiah says that the prophets prophesy falsely, and my people love to have it so. Why do nations so often prefer advisers who tell them what they wish to hear?
Jesus said: a prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house.
The psalm says that the stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
Jeremiah asks: is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?
Yeats wrote after a great war: things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; mere anarchy is loosed upon the world.
The Book of Judges ends: in those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes.

Thomas Hardy wrote in 1914 that the world is as it used to be, all nations striving strong to make red war yet redder. What reason is there to think the ruin of one country is anything but the way of the world?
Jesus said that every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation.
Paul asks: look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
The exiles by the rivers of Babylon sat down and wept when they remembered Zion.
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of those who confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Jeremiah told the exiles: seek the peace of the city, for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
The first letter to Timothy asks prayers for all in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life. In a time of upheaval, is keeping quiet and out of faction a withdrawal or a service?
Confucius said that if the people have no faith in their rulers, there is no standing for the state.
Hosea says in God's name: my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.
The Preacher says: woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning.
Ezekiel cries: woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves.
Jesus said of certain religious teachers: they be blind leaders of the blind.
John Locke argued that the care of souls does not belong to the magistrate. Where should the line run between the clergy and the government of a country?
Isaiah says: O my people, they which lead thee cause thee to err, and destroy the way of thy paths.
Proverbs says that when the righteous are in authority the people rejoice, but when the wicked beareth rule the people mourn.
Mencius said that the people are the most important element in a nation, and the sovereign the lightest.
Plato held that cities will never have rest from their evils until philosophers are kings. What kind of knowledge should those who direct public affairs have?
George Washington allowed that parties in free countries may be useful checks, within certain limits. Are parties themselves the cause of ruin, or only their excess?
Lincoln quoted the Gospel to his own divided country: a house divided against itself cannot stand.
Sa‘di observed that ten dervishes may sleep under the same blanket, but one country cannot hold two padshahs.
James Madison wrote that if men were angels no government would be necessary.
Wordsworth remembered the first days of the French Revolution: bliss was it in that dawn to be alive, but to be young was very heaven. Why do revolutions inspire such hope, and what becomes of it?
Dickens began his novel of revolution: it was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the spring of hope.
Edmund Burke wrote that a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.
Yeats wrote that the best lack all conviction, while the worst are full of passionate intensity.
The Qur’an says that God changeth not the condition of a folk until they first change that which is in their hearts.
Jesus charged the teachers of his day with holding the tradition of men in place of the commandment of God.
The psalm says that except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.
Through Hosea God says: I will be as the dew unto Israel; he shall grow as the lily.
The psalm says that weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
Lamentations says that the Lord's compassions fail not; they are new every morning.
Through Jeremiah God says: I know the thoughts that I think toward you, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
John Stuart Mill called it a pleasant falsehood that truth always triumphs over persecution. On what grounds, then, can one be sure that a country's turmoil will end well?
Habakkuk is told of the vision: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come.
Shelley asks the west wind: if Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?
Isaiah says that the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
Isaiah says: thou shalt be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer of paths to dwell in.
Jesus told his followers: ye are the salt of the earth, and asked what use salt is that has lost its savour.
The Qur’an says of victory and defeat: these are only the vicissitudes which We cause to follow one another for mankind. If every people has its day, what lasts when the day is over?
The psalm says: not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto Thy name give glory.
Paul says that God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
Moses told Israel: the Lord did not set His love upon you because ye were more in number than any people, for ye were the fewest. What does it mean, and not mean, to call a country favoured?
Ezekiel prophesied to the wind, and the breath came into the slain, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet.
Heraclitus said that the way up and the way down is one and the same.
Malachi promises that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
Tennyson's old Ulysses says: though much is taken, much abides, and we are strong in will to strive and not to yield.
George Herbert asks: who would have thought my shrivelled heart could have recovered greenness?

isaiah-to-his-anointed-to-cyrus.text: Thus saith the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him; and I will loose the loins of kings, to open before him the two leaved gates; and the gates shall not be shut

ezra-cyrus-king-of-persia.text: Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The Lord God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the Lord God of Israel, (he is the God,) which is in Jerusalem

judges-right-in-his-own-eyes.text: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes

isaiah-your-country-is-desolate.text: Your country is desolate, your cities are burned with fire: your land, strangers devour it in your presence, and it is desolate, as overthrown by strangers

isaiah-they-which-lead-thee.text: As for my people, children are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, they which lead thee cause thee to err, and destroy the way of thy paths

jeremiah-thoughts-of-peace.text: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end

isaiah-repairer-of-the-breach.text: And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in

nehemiah-let-us-rise-up-and-build.text: Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach. Then I told them of the hand of my God which was good upon me; as also the king's words that he had spoken unto me. And they said, Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for this good work

amos-raise-up-the-tabernacle.text: In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old

saadi-shepherd-for-the-sheep.text: kings exist for protecting subjects and subjects not for obeying kings.' The padshah is the guardian of the dervish Although wealth is in the glory of his reign. The sheep is not for the shepherd But the shepherd for the service of it
saadi-shepherd-for-the-sheep.author: Saʿdī

khayyam-courts-where-jamshyd-gloried.text: They say the Lion and the Lizard keep / The courts where Jamshyd gloried and drank deep: / And Bahram, that great Hunter—the Wild Ass / Stamps o'er his Head, but cannot break his Sleep
khayyam-courts-where-jamshyd-gloried.author: Omar Khayyám
khayyam-courts-where-jamshyd-gloried.caveat: FitzGerald’s version is a free one.
